Doubt: the Fortran as committed is compiled for nx=48, L=288 (Main_stripes_wf.f parameter statement), so for this 256-site instance the program must be edited and recompiled before the script can run. note: parameters = Nsite^2 + alpha + 2 + 2 alpha Nsite = 64^2 + 8 + 2 + 2*8*64 = 5130 COMPLEX parameters (ComplexType 1 in every def file; 10260 real numbers): pair-product orbitals f_ij without sublattice structure (NOrbitalIdx = Nsite^2), RBM hidden biases (alpha), physical-layer biases (2, one per spin), and translation-invariant RBM weights (2 alpha Nsite, the 1x1 RBM sublattice sub_rbm_phidx.py generates, as the method string states). samples = NVMCSample x MPI processes / NSplitSize = 100 x 8 / 1 = 800 per SR step: with NSplitSize = 1 every rank is its own sampling group (vmcmain.c "group1 = rank0/NSplitSize"), draws NVMCSample samples after NVMCWarmUp = 100 (each separated by NVMCInterval x Nsite = 64 proposals) and WeightAverageWE sums the weights over all ranks (average.c); iterations = NSROptItrStep = 1000 SR steps (the parameters are averaged over the last NSROptItrSmp = 100). All of these are the defaults of make_modpara, not overridden by the optimisation call. Each amplitude sums a Pfaffian of the 50-electron pair-product state over NSPGaussLeg x |NMPTrans| = 8 x 64 = 512 spin/momentum projection points. Doubt (why confidence is low): the script is the simplified template of programs/mVMC_makedef/README.txt ("For simplicity, we focus on the case of Ns=8x8"). It runs ONE optimisation stage with the projections and the RBM on from the start, while the README's protocol has three optimisation stages (f_ij alone from the UHF solution, then the RBM, then the projections) whose step counts are not stated anywhere, and it never runs the Lanczos step the energy includes: make_all.py also writes namelist_aft.def/modpara_aft.def (NVMCCalMode=1, NLanczosMode=1, NVMCWarmUp=500, NVMCInterval=5, NVMCSample=5000, NDataQtySmp=10) but mVMC.sh does not call it. So the counts are the script's single stage, not the published run's total. No time is recorded anywhere; "mpiexec -np 8" names MPI processes, not hardware.

As published, Optimizer.optimize() ends with "return res.x" on the circuit object, which has no attribute x, so the first call exits with an AttributeError and "&&" would skip the symmetric run; the step counts are therefore what the code intends, not what it can be shown to have run, hence confidence low. Samples: none; the method string says exact gradients on a state vector. The code has no exact branch that main.py reaches: it draws binomial estimates with the default 2^36 shots (--log2samples default 36), which is exact to about 4e-6 relative. note: Parameters: 64 from the method string (high confidence); the circuit code builds 64 one-parameter gates (SU2_symmetrized._get_dimerizarion_layers: range(1) x 4 shifts x (8 + 8) pairs), which reproduces it. Iterations: 2000 = 1000 natural-gradient steps without symmetry projection, then 1000 continuing with the 64-element projector (n_iter default 1000; main.py is called twice and passes only lr). As published, Optimizer.optimize() ends with "return res.x" on the circuit object, which has no attribute x, so the first call exits with an AttributeError and "&&" would skip the symmetric run; the step counts are therefore what the code intends, not what it can be shown to have run, hence confidence low. Samples: none; the method string says exact gradients on a state vector. The code has no exact branch that main.py reaches: it draws binomial estimates with the default 2^36 shots (--log2samples default 36), which is exact to about 4e-6 relative. The script passes --j2=0.0 with --lattice=triangle4x4, and hamiltonians.HeisenbergTriangle adds the diagonal (third-direction) bonds only "if not np.isclose(j2, 0.0)": as published it simulates the 4x4 square-lattice Heisenberg model (exact -44.914), not the triangular one the row's energy -34.1780764 belongs to (exact -34.222). The step count and circuit are still the code's; the Hamiltonian is not the row's. Provenance: the value entered VarBench in 26f221f (2022-10-18, Nikita Astrakhantsev); the program was added to methods in 6887677 (2024-08-10) ("wip: added the VQE simulator"; next commit "VQE simulator: dusted-off version runs"), so it is a later reconstruction. The VarBench SM (arXiv:2302.04919 Sec. S3 D) describes the ansatz and the natural-gradient update but no step count. No device or time is recorded.

note: Parameters: 64 from the method string (high confidence); the circuit code builds 64 one-parameter gates (SU2_symmetrized._get_dimerizarion_layers: range(1) x 4 shifts x (8 + 8) pairs), which reproduces it. Iterations: 2000 = 1000 natural-gradient steps without symmetry projection, then 1000 continuing with the 128-element projector (n_iter default 1000; main.py is called twice and passes only lr). As published, Optimizer.optimize() ends with "return res.x" on the circuit object, which has no attribute x, so the first call exits with an AttributeError and "&&" would skip the symmetric run; the step counts are therefore what the code intends, not what it can be shown to have run, hence confidence low. Samples: none; the method string says exact gradients on a state vector. The code has no exact branch that main.py reaches: it draws binomial estimates with the default 2^36 shots (--log2samples default 36), which is exact to about 4e-6 relative. Provenance: the value entered VarBench in 5d1ebf9 (2022-11-11, Nikita Astrakhantsev); the program was added to methods in 6887677 (2024-08-10) ("wip: added the VQE simulator"; next commit "VQE simulator: dusted-off version runs"), so it is a later reconstruction. The VarBench SM (arXiv:2302.04919 Sec. S3 D) describes the ansatz and the natural-gradient update but no step count. No device or time is recorded.

No device or time is recorded (the conda env includes CUDA; the README says a GPU is "usually needed for VMC on larger lattices", which is not a statement about these runs).

reported_as: Sec. III.C.1: Our standard ACE architecture, trained without explicit symmetries, achieves a ground-state energy of −0.76464(1). This result is already more accurate than that of HFPS [23] while requiring only one-fifteenth of the cost. By directly optimizing the projected, symmetrized state reach a new state-of-the-art energy of −0.76623(1). This surpasses the previous best result −0.766073(6) from NNBF [25] with only one-sixth of the computational cost. Additionally, a GFMC calculation with the ACE trial wave-function gives an even lower energy of −0.76647(2). ... Appendix B: In the first stage, we perform 3×10^4 initial steps without enforcing any symmetry. ... First, we restore D2 and spin inversion symmetry and train for 4×10^3 steps. Next, we additionally restore the half-translation symmetries and train for another 4×10^3 steps. Finally, we restore the 1/4-translational symmetries and train for 10^3 steps. ... Table V (Hyperparameters for the MARCH optimizer): Learning rate schedule (t): ACE 10^-1 (1 + max(t−1000,0)/4000)^-1, SCALE 5×10^-1 (1 + max(t−1000,0)/8000)^-1; Optimizer momentum (µ,β) 0.95, 0.995; Damping (λ) 0.001; Batch size clip(32 Lx×Ly, 4096, 8192); Local energy clipping 5.0; MCMC steps per sample 2.5 Lx×Ly; Total optimization steps 50000. Shared parameters apply to both models. ... reported_as: Sec. III (Optimizing multi-determinants): As shown in Fig. 3, for the n_h = 2048 model, optimization with four symmetries improves the energy by 29% (43% after full projection), optimization with the 32 symmetries improves the energy by 54% (67% after full projection), and optimization with all 512 symmetries improves the energy by 75% relative to the single MLP ansatz with same n_h. These additional optimizations all use the single-determinant NNBF as a starting point and, in total, take approximately 200, 800, and 3000 GPU hours respectively. [...] The HFPS reaches an energy of -0.76413 which is somewhat higher then the -0.76486(2) of our symmetry optimization with 32 determinants. Additionally, our result can be further projected at essentially no cost to the fully symmetric state to reach an energy of -0.76560(1) [...] The optimization of our 32 determinant MLP-NNBF is faster by approximately a factor of 2 compared with the HFPS. || Sec. II.B: All optimizations reported in this paper were performed using H100 GPUs on GH200 superchips. Most optimizations were performed using a single H100 GPU, but longer optimizations were parallelized across 4 GPUs. GPU times are reported as cumulative GPU usage (e.g. parallelized times are 4 times the wall clock time). All optimization times include the cumulative cost of optimization for a given point which includes (where specified) optimizing smaller ansatz first. || Appendix B: Unless otherwise specified, the total number of markov chains is fixed at N_s = 1024 and the learning rate is fixed at 3 x 10^-4. We first train the single particle orbitals without backflow for 10^5 VMC iterations. [...] The training for the data in Fig. A1 took 3 x 10^6 VMC iterations, followed by 5 x 10^5 VMC iterations with an exponential decay learning rate schedule tuning the learning rate to 10^-7. The training for the model with 4 symmetries took approximately 8 x 10^5 VMC iterations, while the training for the model with 32 symmetries took approximately 5 x 10^5 VMC iterations. || Sec. II.A: Our MLP is fully connected with two hidden layers each followed by a layer normalization and relu activation. || Sec. II.A: u(n) is the output, an N\times L matrix, of an MLP with input n [...] Here both spin sectors are combined into a single matrix (e.g. N is the sum of the spin up and down electrons and L is twice the number of physical sites) [...] Our MLP is fully connected with two hidden layers each followed by a layer normalization and relu activation. The input layer is set by |n> = |n_0, n_1, ..., n_L> where n_i \in {-1,1} denotes an empty or occupied spin orbital. The last output layer contains a bias but no non-linear function; this bias can be interpreted as a fixed mean-field solution onto which the neural network provides additive configuration-dependent backflow corrections. || Sec. III: A fixed depth multi-layer MLP-NNBF scales as O(n_o n_h + n_h^2 + \alpha n_h n_o^2 + (\alpha n_o)^3) per step where n_o is the number of orbitals and \alpha is the filling fraction. For our system, n_o = L = 128 and \alpha = 0.4375. [...] this crossover happens at n_h = 7168 || Sec. III (PNNBF): U(n) and J(n) are both L\times L matrices output by the MLP (e.g. the last layer of the network has 2L^2 nodes) || App. B: We then multiply all single particle orbitals by a factor of 10^3, set them to the bias of the last layer of the MLP, and randomly initialize the weights to form the initial MLP-NNBF ansatz. || Fig. A2 caption: Each VMC sweep reports the average energy from 100 VMC steps of each of the 1024 VMC chains. || Acknowledgements: The NQS simulations are implemented using internally developed code with JAX [43], Flax [44], and Optax [45]. || Abstract: We explore efficient ways to generate these multi-determinant expansions without increasing the number of variational parameters. || Sec. III: Here we optimize the energy of Eq. 5 using the parameters of a single MLP using different sets of symmetries including the 4 point group symmetries; 32 symmetries by adding in spin inversion and half translation symmetries; and 512 symmetries by including all translations. || Eq. 5: \Psi_sym(n) = \sum_g \Pi(n,g) \Psi(gn), where g \in G and \Pi(n,g) = \pm 1 is an additional sign coming from fermion permutations.

reported_as: In our implementation, a two-layer MLP with 8192 neurons reaches an energy of -0.76258(1) within 400 GPU hours. This energy is lower than recent results using a tensor backflow ansatz with a Lanczos step [24]. [...] All optimizations reported in this paper were performed using H100 GPUs on GH200 superchips. Most optimizations were performed using a single H100 GPU, but longer optimizations were parallelized across 4 GPUs. GPU times are reported as cumulative GPU usage [...] Unless otherwise specified, the total number of markov chains is fixed at N_s = 1024 and the learning rate is fixed at 3e-4. We first train the single particle orbitals without backflow for 10^5 VMC iterations. [...] The training for the data in Fig. A1 took 3 x 10^6 VMC iterations, followed by 5 x 10^5 VMC iterations with an exponential decay learning rate schedule tuning the learning rate to 1e-7. || Sec. II.A: u(n) is the output, an N\times L matrix, of an MLP with input n [...] Here both spin sectors are combined into a single matrix (e.g. N is the sum of the spin up and down electrons and L is twice the number of physical sites) [...] Our MLP is fully connected with two hidden layers each followed by a layer normalization and relu activation. The input layer is set by |n> = |n_0, n_1, ..., n_L> where n_i \in {-1,1} denotes an empty or occupied spin orbital. The last output layer contains a bias but no non-linear function; this bias can be interpreted as a fixed mean-field solution onto which the neural network provides additive configuration-dependent backflow corrections. || Sec. III: A fixed depth multi-layer MLP-NNBF scales as O(n_o n_h + n_h^2 + \alpha n_h n_o^2 + (\alpha n_o)^3) per step where n_o is the number of orbitals and \alpha is the filling fraction. For our system, n_o = L = 128 and \alpha = 0.4375. [...] this crossover happens at n_h = 7168 || Sec. III (PNNBF): U(n) and J(n) are both L\times L matrices output by the MLP (e.g. the last layer of the network has 2L^2 nodes) || App. B: We then multiply all single particle orbitals by a factor of 10^3, set them to the bias of the last layer of the MLP, and randomly initialize the weights to form the initial MLP-NNBF ansatz. || Fig. A2 caption: Each VMC sweep reports the average energy from 100 VMC steps of each of the 1024 VMC chains. || Acknowledgements: The NQS simulations are implemented using internally developed code with JAX [43], Flax [44], and Optax [45].

We used 4096 Monte Carlo samples and GCNNs with 4 (8) layers of 6 feature maps each for the 36- (108-) site simulations. II A: All GCNN ansätze used in this work have a fixed number of feature maps in every layer, connected by real-valued kernels K, W. In most cases, we restrict the embedding kernels K to the local clusters shown in Fig. 1. We also impose locality on the convolutional kernels W: these are only nonzero for g = t p, where p is a point-group symmetry that leaves the origin in place, and t is a translation by a lattice vector indicated in Fig. 1. || FIG. 1.
